blocks.text:
Section: GRADUATE METHOD
Source mapping: original slide(s) 2, 5, 19.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
Consider the statement that our program printed 42. It reports an observation, but it does not specify the input domain, the compiler assumptions, or whether an invalid memory access occurred on the way to that output. A stronger argument separates a contract, assumptions, and evidence. The contract says what counts as correct. Assumptions identify the conditions under which the reasoning applies. Evidence is what we inspected or measured.

These categories prevent two common mistakes. First, a useful test result is not a universal proof. Second, a documented guarantee is not a measured performance result. During the lecture, attach each conclusion to its boundary: language, binary interface, operating system, or hardware. If the observation conflicts with the prediction, revise the model or inspect a lower-level artifact rather than inventing a promise that the interface never made. This framework is an instructional elaboration of the original chapter's contract model.

Sixth-grade explanation
Do not stop at “it worked.” Say what you expected, what had to be true, and what you checked.

Discussion / pause
What is missing from the claim “the executable ran successfully”?

Expected response: The success criterion, input domain, environmental assumptions, and evidence beyond that one run.

Transition: Hardware: compute, state, and movement.

topics.summary: The original chapter begins with a deliberately simplified CPU-memory-I/O model. blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.1.1 · HARDWARE & SOFTWARE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 3.

Graduate lecture narration
The original chapter begins with a deliberately simplified CPU-memory-I/O model. CPU cores execute instructions, registers hold working state, memory holds addressable instructions and data, and controllers connect devices to the rest of the machine. Storage and peripherals have different purposes and access mechanisms from registers. Buses and interconnects carry requests and data among these components.

Use this picture to ask three questions: where does a value currently exist, which component initiates its movement, and what event tells another component that progress occurred? The picture is not a claim that contemporary processors execute one instruction at a time or that all transfers pass through one physical wire. It is a model of responsibilities. The software side supplies instructions and data, while the language, executable format, operating system, and device interface assign meaning to particular encodings. A sequence of bits does not identify its own type or purpose.

Sixth-grade explanation
The processor does the work. Registers and memory hold information. Controllers help the computer talk to storage and other devices.

Discussion / pause
Does a byte sequence tell you whether it is an instruction, an integer, or text?

Expected response: No. Its interpretation depends on the surrounding interface, representation, and execution context.

Transition: Follow the value—not just the statement.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.1.1 · CPU, REGISTERS & MEMORY
Source mapping: original slide(s) 3, 18.

Graduate lecture narration
Suppose a source expression adds three to a value. Before discussing the addition, ask how the value became available to the executing instruction. It might arrive in an argument register, come from a prior calculation, or require a load. The result might remain in a register, be used immediately, or be stored. This is why a source variable should not automatically be imagined as a permanently assigned RAM slot.

The instruction stream also has to be fetched. Therefore, saying that an addition needs no data-memory access is not the same as saying that the processor uses no memory-related machinery. The original chapter makes this distinction in its expression example. Our register-workbench analogy explains placement, not exact timing or physical implementation. At this stage, track architectural inputs and outputs and leave detailed cache behavior and processor scheduling to later chapters.

Sixth-grade explanation
Think of registers as a tiny workbench and memory as a larger set of shelves. A value may already be on the workbench when it is needed.

Discussion / pause
Can the addition itself avoid a data-memory load?

Expected response: Yes, when the needed operand is already in a register or the compiler can otherwise supply it without a load.

Transition: Controllers and interrupts coordinate I/O.

---

topics.title: Controllers and interrupts coordinate I/O
topics.summary: I/O introduces a boundary between requesting work and completing work. A controller supplies a device-facing interface. Systems software translates a higher-level request into actions the device supports. An interrupt is one mechanism by which the system can learn that an event needs attention; it should not be mistaken for the application itself performing the hardware operation.

blocks.title: Student slide 6: source text
items: Identify who initiates movement, who performs it, and who reports completion.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.1.1 · STORAGE & PERIPHERALS
Source mapping: original slide(s) 3, 12.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
I/O introduces a boundary between requesting work and completing work. A controller supplies a device-facing interface. Systems software translates a higher-level request into actions the device supports. An interrupt is one mechanism by which the system can learn that an event needs attention; it should not be mistaken for the application itself performing the hardware operation.

A useful explanation identifies the requester, the component doing the transfer, and the component reporting completion. Do not silently assume that a library call corresponds to one device command or that returning from a high-level call means durable storage has been achieved. Those are separate contracts. The source deck names controllers and interrupts; this slide makes the request/completion distinction explicit without prescribing one device protocol. We will revisit the same distinction when we discuss buffered output and partial failures.

Sixth-grade explanation
A device does not always finish right away. The program asks for work, the device does it, and the system reports what happened.

Transition: Software role is not execution privilege.

topics.title: Software role is not execution privilege
topics.summary: The chapter classifies systems software by role: kernels control resources, compilers translate, linkers connect compiled units, runtime libraries supply startup and shared operations, and drivers handle device-specific interactions. Application software performs tasks for users or services. The distinction is useful, but not absolute. A database application may contain its own allocator, scheduler, or storage engine.

blocks.title: Student slide 7: source text

Often executes inside the application process
Placement depends on the OS architecture

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.1.2–1.1.3 · SOFTWARE CATEGORIES
Source mapping: original slide(s) 4.

Graduate lecture narration
The chapter classifies systems software by role: kernels control resources, compilers translate, linkers connect compiled units, runtime libraries supply startup and shared operations, and drivers handle device-specific interactions. Application software performs tasks for users or services. The distinction is useful, but not absolute. A database application may contain its own allocator, scheduler, or storage engine.

Execution privilege is a different axis. A compiler is systems software that normally executes as an ordinary user process. A server may manage important information without becoming kernel code. Conversely, a particular driver architecture can place components on either side of a privilege boundary. Avoid using the labels low-level, systems, and privileged as synonyms. For diagnosis, ask what a component is responsible for and what operations it is authorized to perform. These questions may have different answers.

Sixth-grade explanation
Some programs help the computer run other programs. That does not mean they all get special permission to control the machine.

Discussion / pause
Why does a compiler not need kernel privilege just because it is systems software?

Expected response: Translation is its role; the OS can provide ordinary process permissions sufficient to read inputs and write outputs.

Transition: An abstraction is a smaller contract.

---

blocks.text:
Section: 1.1.4 · ABSTRACTION LAYERS
Source mapping: original slide(s) 5.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The original slide describes an abstraction as hiding detail while preserving a contract. For example, a file descriptor lets a caller request byte-oriented I/O without manipulating a storage controller. A vector presents a sequence while hiding many allocation decisions. Hidden details continue to exist; they are simply not all part of the caller's interface.

At graduate level, describe a contract using preconditions, permitted effects, postconditions, and failure behavior. Preconditions tell the caller what must already hold. Postconditions constrain the result when the operation succeeds. Failure behavior says what may have changed and what remains valid. This is a reasoning framework, not a claim that every real interface documents all of these perfectly. A missing or ambiguous guarantee is something to investigate, not permission to assume convenient behavior. Abstraction succeeds when the smaller contract is sufficient for the caller's reasoning.

Sixth-grade explanation
A button can be easy to use even when the machine behind it is complicated. You still need to know what pressing the button promises.

Transition: Guaranteed, customary, or measured?.

topics.summary: Separate what an interface promises from what an implementation commonly does and from what you observed on a particular run. This distinction appears explicitly in the source chapter. Suppose an output operation reports that it accepted some number of bytes. The count is part of that operation's result. Whether all bytes were accepted at once, when physical storage was updated, and how long the operation took are different questions.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.1.4 · DO NOT INVENT GUARANTEES
Source mapping: original slide(s) 5, 15, 19.

Graduate lecture narration
Separate what an interface promises from what an implementation commonly does and from what you observed on a particular run. This distinction appears explicitly in the source chapter. Suppose an output operation reports that it accepted some number of bytes. The count is part of that operation's result. Whether all bytes were accepted at once, when physical storage was updated, and how long the operation took are different questions.

The vector example has the same structure: a sequence interface need not expose every allocation decision. A caller who relies on an undocumented growth choice turns an implementation detail into a hidden dependency. When presenting evidence, use precise wording. Say that a run took a measured amount of time under a stated setup, not that the API promises that latency. Say that a platform documents a behavior when it actually does. The method is to classify a claim before relying on it.

Sixth-grade explanation
A rule, a habit, and something you saw once are different. A program should not treat them as the same thing.

Transition: API, ABI, and ISA answer different questions.

Supporting primary sources

topics.title: API, ABI, and ISA answer different questions
topics.summary: An API is a source-facing interface: names, operations, argument meanings, and behavioral contracts. An ABI governs compiled interoperability: calling conventions, register use, data layout, and other binary rules. An ISA describes machine operations and software-visible architectural state. These boundaries answer different questions even when one program crosses all three in a few instructions.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.1.5 · HARDWARE / SOFTWARE INTERFACES
Source mapping: original slide(s) 6.

Graduate lecture narration
An API is a source-facing interface: names, operations, argument meanings, and behavioral contracts. An ABI governs compiled interoperability: calling conventions, register use, data layout, and other binary rules. An ISA describes machine operations and software-visible architectural state. These boundaries answer different questions even when one program crosses all three in a few instructions.

Use a function call as the running example. Its source declaration tells the compiler how the call is written and typed. Binary conventions tell caller and callee where to put arguments and results. The selected machine instructions must then be valid for the target architecture. Matching at one boundary does not imply matching at the others. The original chapter's three warnings remain important: identical APIs do not imply binary compatibility; a shared ISA does not imply a shared ABI; and a shared ISA does not imply identical microarchitecture or speed.

Source mapping: original slide(s) 6.

blocks.text:
Section: 1.1.5 · ISA VS. MICROARCHITECTURE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 3, 6, 18, 19.

Graduate lecture narration
The chapter warns that an ISA and a microarchitecture are not the same thing. The ISA defines the software-visible operations and state that an implementation must honor. Microarchitecture concerns how a particular implementation realizes that behavior. The existence of the same instruction in two systems does not establish the same latency, throughput, cache behavior, or resource contention.

Keep two explanations separate. A functional explanation asks which architectural result an instruction produces under its specified conditions. A performance explanation asks how long a workload takes on a particular implementation and why. A correct functional trace does not provide enough information to derive whole-program timing. Conversely, a favorable benchmark cannot excuse an invalid instruction assumption or a violated language rule. This distinction prepares the performance discussion without turning Chapter 1 into a processor-design course.

Sixth-grade explanation
Two cars can follow the same road rules but have different engines. Two processors can run the same commands at different speeds.

Transition: Locate the boundary before proposing a fix.

blocks.text:
Section: 1.2 · FROM SOURCE TO EXECUTION
Source mapping: original slide(s) 7.

Graduate lecture narration
The source chapter presents a seven-stage model: source, preprocessing, compilation, assembly, linking, loading, and execution. The model separates responsibilities; it does not require every implementation to launch a separate operating-system process for every stage. Compiler drivers often orchestrate several stages in a single command.

Each stage changes what kind of evidence is available. Source text exposes the programmer's operations and obligations. Preprocessed text exposes the translation unit after directives and macros. Assembly exposes symbolic target operations. An object file exposes encoded data, symbols, and relocation requirements. A linked executable describes a loadable program, while loading and runtime establish and exercise the process environment. Notice that passing an earlier stage does not guarantee passing later stages. Successful compilation does not supply an omitted definition, and successful loading does not guarantee that a runtime resource will be available.

Sixth-grade explanation
The program goes through several stations before and while it runs. Each station has a different job and can find a different kind of problem.

Transition: Source code describes an abstract computation.

Supporting primary sources
[GCC] GCC manual, Overall Options. Compilation stages and the -E, -S, -c, and -o compiler-driver options. https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Overall-Options.html

Section: 1.2.1 · SOURCE-LEVEL CONTRACT
Source mapping: original slide(s) 8.

Graduate lecture narration
Before imagining instructions, identify the source-level semantics. The original chapter lists types, expressions, statements, lifetimes, synchronization rules, and observable behavior. These constrain the abstract computation, but source order is not a literal physical schedule. A correct implementation may transform the computation while preserving the behavior required by the language and the implementation's documented guarantees.

For a pointer access, ask whether the object exists, whether the access is in range, and whether its lifetime and synchronization obligations hold. For arithmetic, ask whether the result is representable under the relevant rules. These are not optional details to check after performance tuning. They define the domain in which the rest of the explanation is valid. The public C committee draft provides a reference for abstract-machine reasoning; the lab retains the source deck's C17 compilation mode.

Sixth-grade explanation
Code has rules about what values mean and when they may be used. The computer may organize the work differently while keeping the promised result.

Transition: Not all language uncertainty is undefined behavior.

Section: 1.2.2 · PREPROCESSOR COUNTEREXAMPLE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 9.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
This is a deliberately invalid example for analysis, not a program to use as a numerical experiment. The SQUARE macro replaces its parameter in two positions. Giving it i++ expands the increment expression twice. In C, the two modifications shown in the multiplication expression are unsequenced relative to one another, so the example has undefined behavior. There is no correct portable numeric answer to predict.

Parentheses are still useful in macros because they prevent some precedence surprises, but they do not make repeated evaluation safe. A function that receives an already computed value separates the caller's side effect from the body calculation. Even then, arithmetic range requirements remain: replacing the macro with a function does not make arbitrary signed multiplication overflow valid. This extension turns the source deck's warning about duplicated side effects into a concrete contract failure.

Sixth-grade explanation
A macro can copy your instruction more than once. Asking it to “use the number and then increase it” can accidentally copy the increase too.

Discussion / pause
What portable value should we predict for y?

Expected response: None. The shown expanded expression violates C sequencing rules.

Section: 1.2.2 · TRANSLATION UNITS
Source mapping: original slide(s) 9, 16.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
In the chapter's two-file program, sum.h declares add, sum.c defines it, and main.c calls it. The declaration lets each translation unit check source-level uses. The compiled caller can still depend on a definition that will be supplied later. That is the central reason a program may compile and then fail at the link stage.

The graduate nuance is that a header is not intrinsically declaration-only. Headers can also contain definitions, subject to language and linkage rules. Our teaching layout places this externally linked function's declaration in the header and its definition in one source file. The include guard in the companion lab is an added organizational aid. blocks.text:
Section: 1.2.4 · ASSEMBLY & OBJECT FILES
Source mapping: original slide(s) 10, 11.

Graduate lecture narration
Assembly output is not a uniform list of executable instructions. It can contain labels, directives, data, and symbolic references. Labels identify positions or symbols; directives tell the assembler how to organize material. The assembler encodes instructions and data and emits the additional object-file information required for later stages.

A relocatable object can contain a reference whose final address is not yet known. Keeping that information is not a failure to assemble the file. It is part of separate compilation. The chapter's caller can therefore assemble before the linker sees the definition of add. When reading assembly or disassembly, separate the actual instructions from organizational metadata. When examining an object, ask both what bytes it already contains and what obligations remain unresolved. This is the bridge between compiler output and linking.

Sixth-grade explanation
Assembly uses readable names for machine operations. The assembler makes the bytes and keeps information needed to connect unfinished references later.

Transition: Linking connects separate compiled responsibilities.

Supporting primary sources
[AS] GNU assembler manual, Symbols. Symbolic assembly information retained for later stages. https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/as/Symbols.html
[ELF] System V generic ABI, Relocation. Relocation entries; processor-specific interpretation. The lecture arithmetic is an explicitly illustrative model. https://refspecs.linuxfoundation.org/elf/gabi4+/ch4.reloc.html

Source mapping: original slide(s) 11, 16, 17.

Graduate lecture narration

blocks.text:
Section: 1.2.5 · GRADUATE WORKED MODEL
Source mapping: original slide(s) 11.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
Relocation records preserve information needed to adjust address-dependent content. To make the arithmetic visible, use an illustrative PC-relative relocation model with a symbol address S, an addend A, and a relocation-place address P. Under the chosen model, the stored result is S plus A minus P. For the slide's hexadecimal values, 0x1200 minus 0x1000 gives 0x0200, or 512 decimal.

This is explicitly a teaching model, not the exact encoding of a particular call instruction. Real relocation types define which location P denotes, how an addend is stored, the field width, alignment, and overflow constraints. Some instruction encodings require an addend that accounts for the relationship between the relocation field and the next instruction. The important conceptual result is that assembly can preserve a solvable equation without knowing its final numeric answer. A processor-specific ABI supplies the exact rule.

Sixth-grade explanation
A reference can say “fill in the distance to this function later.” Once the function has a final location, the linker can calculate the distance.

Discussion / pause
Why can the assembler emit a valid object before S is known?

Expected response: It records the unresolved symbol and relocation information so a later stage can compute the needed value.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.2.5–1.2.6 · LINK-TIME VS. LOAD-TIME WORK
Source mapping: original slide(s) 11, 12.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The original chapter mentions both link-time relocation and dynamic loaders that can finish runtime linking. The distinction is timing and packaging, not a choice between having contracts and having none. Static linking selects needed material from object inputs and archives into the output. Dynamic linking leaves shared-object dependencies and associated work for the runtime environment.

A dynamically linked executable can be well formed and still fail to start when a required shared object cannot be found or is incompatible. Likewise, successfully finding a shared library does not establish that the application will handle its later inputs correctly. Do not say that static linking universally means every operating-system dependency disappears, or that every dynamic symbol must always resolve at exactly the same moment. Policies differ. The teaching goal is to identify which obligations remain after the static link stage.

Sixth-grade explanation
Some program pieces are joined before the program runs. Other pieces are found and connected when the program starts or later.

Transition: Loading establishes the executable process image.

Supporting primary sources

[DYNL] Linux man-pages, ld.so(8). Shared-object discovery and dynamic-loader behavior. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ld.so.8.html

Section: 1.2.6 · LOADING
Source mapping: original slide(s) 12.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
Loading connects an executable file to the process that will execute it. The source chapter describes mappings and possible dynamic-loader work. For our Linux teaching environment, execve replaces the current process image with a new program image; it should not be described as creating a new process by itself. Process creation and image replacement are distinct operations.

Executable metadata describes what must be mapped and how execution begins. For ELF, program headers describe segments relevant to loading; these should not be confused with the section-oriented view used by many link and inspection operations. A dynamic interpreter may also be involved. This is a deliberately bounded Linux/ELF elaboration, not a universal sequence for every operating system. Successful loading establishes a starting environment, not the future availability of all files, permissions, sockets, or memory allocations the program will request.

A program file is not yet a running program. The system must set up its memory view and starting conditions first.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.2.6 · DEMAND PAGING
Source mapping: original slide(s) 12.

Graduate lecture narration
The original chapter explicitly separates mapping from residency. A mapping establishes a relationship in the process's virtual address space. It does not necessarily mean every mapped page already has its contents resident in physical memory. With demand paging, an access may cause the operating system to make a page available before the program continues.

Therefore, a page fault is not automatically evidence of an invalid program. Some faults are part of normal demand handling. An invalid access or a protection violation is a different case and can cause failure. For measurement, a first access can have different costs from a later access, so a benchmark should state whether initialization and first-touch effects are included. That last point is a reasoning consequence of the mapping/residency distinction, not a claim that every page fault requires disk I/O.

Sixth-grade explanation
Having a place on the map does not mean the page is already on your desk. The system may bring it into memory only when you first use it.

Discussion / pause
Does mapping a large file prove that every byte has already been read into RAM?

Expected response: No. Mapping and current physical residency are different properties.

Transition: Runtime begins before main and extends through termination.

Supporting primary sources
[MMAP] Linux man-pages, mmap(2). Virtual mappings and population-related behavior; lecture distinguishes mapping from residency. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/mmap.2.html

Section: 1.2.7 · RUNTIME EXECUTION
Source mapping: original slide(s) 12.

Graduate lecture narration
A hosted program's runtime story does not begin and end with the first and last lines of main. Startup establishes the language and library environment. The program then executes its own code and library code, sometimes requesting kernel services through system calls. Scheduling can interrupt its progress or delay when it resumes. The source deck makes these boundaries part of the chapter rather than treating them as hidden trivia.

Termination also has a contract. Normal library termination and abrupt process termination do not necessarily perform the same user-space cleanup. Section: WORKED EXAMPLE · GNU BINARY TOOLS
Source mapping: original slide(s) 11, 17.

Graduate lecture narration
An artifact inspection is strongest when it answers a specific question. nm shows symbols, so use it to connect an undefined reference in the caller with a definition in the other object. blocks.text:
Section: WORKED EXAMPLE · CONTROLLED FAILURE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 11, 17, 20.

Graduate lecture narration
A controlled failure is useful because it changes one obligation at a time. The caller was compiled with a visible declaration, so its source-level call can be accepted. Now intentionally omit sum.o from the final command. The missing definition of add prevents the ordinary executable link from completing. This was tested during preparation and failed as expected with a diagnostic mentioning add.

Do not demand identical diagnostic wording across compilers and linkers. The stable prediction is the failed link and its relationship to the omitted definition. Reintroducing sum.o addresses that specific obligation. Adding another header include to main.c does not supply the missing compiled body. Nor does this experiment show that every undefined-reference problem has the same cause: symbol spelling, linkage, and binary compatibility can matter in more complex builds. Here the intentionally omitted object isolates the cause.

Leave out the piece that defines add. The caller can still be compiled, but the linker cannot finish the whole program.

blocks.text:
Section: WORKED EXAMPLE · PREDICT BEFORE REBUILDING
Source mapping: original slide(s) 20.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The original guided lab asks students to change one function and predict which artifacts should change. For our ordinary separate-compilation model, changing sum.c requires rebuilding sum.o and relinking the executable. Changing the shared declaration in sum.h can affect both translation units that include it, so both objects need to be reconsidered. A main.c edit similarly affects its own object and the final link.

These are dependency obligations, not guarantees of different output bytes. Recompilation can produce identical bytes when a change does not affect the result, and timestamps or build metadata can change for unrelated reasons. When one part changes, rebuild the parts that depend on it. A change to shared instructions can affect more than one source file.

blocks.text:
Section: WORKED EXAMPLE · SOURCE-LEVEL REASONING
Source mapping: original slide(s) 8, 18.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The original expression is int y = x + 3. Begin with a valid int value x and a context in which reading it is permitted. For the mathematical result to be representable as int, x must not exceed INT_MAX minus three. Adding a positive three to any representable x cannot cross the lower bound, so the upper bound is the interesting arithmetic condition here.

Under those assumptions, the source-level postcondition is that y has the mathematical value of x plus three. That is the claim the implementation must realize when the result matters. The variable can be optimized away if the surrounding program has no required observable use for it. This sequence of reasoning deliberately precedes instruction selection. It prevents the mistaken argument that a familiar hardware addition or a successful test somehow establishes valid source semantics for every possible input.

Sixth-grade explanation
Before adding three, check that the starting value is allowed and the answer fits. A good-looking answer does not fix a broken rule.

Expected response: For a valid int x, adding positive 3 cannot make the mathematical result smaller than INT_MIN.

The original chapter organizes systems programming around six concerns rather than a single language feature or level of privilege. Low-level reasoning addresses representation and machine behavior. blocks.text:
Section: 1.3.2 · PERFORMANCE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 13, 19.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The chapter names latency and throughput as separate performance concerns. Latency measures a completion interval for a chosen unit of work. Throughput counts completed work per unit time. Improving one does not logically establish an improvement in the other; the workload and measurement boundary matter.

For a simple single-thread observation, partition a chosen elapsed interval into time running on the CPU, time blocked, and time runnable but waiting for CPU service. Under this teaching model, those states are mutually exclusive and account for the interval. The illustrative values total twelve milliseconds. They are not measurements of the companion program. The point is diagnostic: optimizing instructions cannot remove time that the thread spends waiting for a resource or scheduling opportunity. For multiple threads, sums of CPU time and elapsed wall time require more care because work can overlap.

Sixth-grade explanation
Latency is how long one job takes. Throughput is how many jobs finish in a period. A job can also spend time waiting instead of working.

Transition: Derive the limit of a local speedup.

Section: 1.3.2 · GRADUATE PERFORMANCE DERIVATION
Source mapping: original slide(s) 13, 19.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
This derivation makes the chapter's performance concern quantitative without pretending that a local optimization accelerates the entire system equally. Normalize the original total time to one. Assume that sixty percent belongs to a component we can make three times faster and that the remaining forty percent is unchanged. The new time is 0.60 divided by three plus 0.40, or 0.60 of the original total. Overall speedup is therefore one divided by 0.60, about 1.67.

The assumptions are the substance of the argument: the same work is performed, the fractions come from the same baseline, the portions do not overlap in this simplified account, and no new overhead appears. Section: 1.3.2 · MEASUREMENT DESIGN
Source mapping: original slide(s) 19.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The original chapter states that performance claims require measurement. The graduate extension is to specify what another person would need to reproduce the claim. Define the workload, input sizes, correctness criterion, and unit of work. Record the compiler and relevant options, the platform, and whether initialization and first-touch effects are included. Repeat the measurement and report variability rather than selecting a single favorable number.

This is a proposed experimental protocol, not a claim that all benchmarks require one rigid recipe. For a program with external services, the environment may be difficult to control, so the report must describe those limitations. A fair comparison also separates instrumented correctness builds from performance builds. Sanitizers change the program being measured. Before timing an optimization, confirm that both candidates meet the intended semantic contract; otherwise, the benchmark compares different or invalid work.

Sixth-grade explanation
A fair speed test uses the same job and records the conditions. Repeat it, because one run may be unusually fast or slow.

blocks.text:
Section: 1.3.3 · RESOURCE MANAGEMENT
Source mapping: original slide(s) 14.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The chapter says every acquisition needs an owner, a validity interval, and a release rule. Think of memory, file descriptors, handles, or other resources as obligations that persist beyond one successful function call. The operation that acquires a resource may differ from the component responsible for releasing it, but that transfer must be explicit.

The original invariant owner(fd) equals exactly one component is a design policy, not an automatic property of the operating system. References can be shared, descriptors can be duplicated, and ownership protocols can vary. What must remain unambiguous is the release responsibility for each owned resource. A borrowed reference should not silently acquire permission to release the underlying resource. Diagram the lifecycle before writing complicated error paths. That often reveals leaks, double release, and use after the agreed validity interval.

Sixth-grade explanation
When a program borrows something, someone must be responsible for returning it. Passing it to another part must pass that responsibility clearly.

Transition: Partial initialization is where cleanup is tested.

Section: 1.3.3 · FAILURE DURING ACQUISITION
Source mapping: original slide(s) 14, 15.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
A straight-line success path hides much of resource management's difficulty. Suppose an operation first acquires a file descriptor and then allocates a buffer. If the buffer allocation fails, the descriptor still needs its release path. If the first acquisition fails, neither resource should be treated as acquired. If all work succeeds, both must be released or intentionally transferred according to the contract.

The table is a design exercise rather than a complete implementation of any particular operating-system cleanup routine. It makes the state of each resource explicit at each boundary. Reverse-order cleanup is often natural for nested dependencies, but the dependency contract—not a slogan—determines the necessary order. Release operations can themselves have API-specific behavior, which should not be hidden by calling every cleanup step infallible. The source chapter's phrase partial success becomes a concrete state-accounting problem here.

Sixth-grade explanation
A program may get the first thing it needs but fail to get the second. It must return only what it actually borrowed.

Transition: Invariants state what remains true at boundaries.

Section: 1.3.3–1.3.4 · CORRECTNESS
Source mapping: original slide(s) 14.

Graduate lecture narration
The three original invariant examples represent different kinds of correctness obligations. A buffer bound constrains numeric state. A single-owner policy constrains resource responsibility. A set of allowed work-item states constrains the lifecycle model. None is useful merely because it appears in a comment; each must be connected to operations that establish, preserve, or intentionally transition the state.

Define the boundaries at which the invariant must hold. An operation can temporarily rearrange internal state while holding exclusive access, but it must reestablish the public invariant before exposing the object under its contract. Concurrent access complicates that reasoning, so do not assume that writing an assert makes an operation synchronized. Correctness is relative to a specification and assumptions. Section: 1.3.4 · PRECONDITIONS, POSTCONDITIONS & FRAME
Source mapping: original slide(s) 14.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
Assume data designates a writable array of capacity bytes, used is valid non-overlapping metadata, zero is at most used and used is at most capacity, and the operation has exclusive access. The full case returns without changing the abstract buffer state. Otherwise, used is strictly smaller than capacity, so indexing data at used is in bounds. blocks.text:
Section: 1.3.5 · CONTROLLED FAILURE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 15.

Graduate lecture narration
Robustness is not the assertion that nothing can go wrong. The source chapter describes invalid input, unavailable resources, interruptions, and partial failures as conditions that should lead to controlled behavior. A robust specification explains the result, the state that remains, and the obligations still owned by the caller or callee.

For a failed operation, ask three practical questions. What changed before the failure was reported? Which resources are still valid and who owns them? Is retry safe, and from which point? These questions connect robustness to the invariants and ownership model rather than treating error handling as a message printed at the end. Section: 1.3.6 · PORTABILITY
Source mapping: original slide(s) 15.

Graduate lecture narration
The original chapter explicitly distinguishes source portability, binary compatibility, and performance portability. Source portability concerns whether the program can be translated appropriately for another supported environment. Binary compatibility concerns whether compiled components can interoperate or execute under the expected machine and runtime conventions. Performance portability concerns whether the implementation still meets the relevant performance goals across platforms.

These are related but independent claims. A portable source program may need rebuilding. A binary can require a particular ABI or shared library. A program that executes correctly may have different bottlenecks on a second implementation. Make each platform assumption visible and testable: representation, interfaces, resource limits, compiler options, and runtime dependencies. Do not call a design portable without specifying the supported environments and the level of portability being claimed.

Sixth-grade explanation
Code that can be rebuilt elsewhere, a file that runs elsewhere, and a program that stays fast elsewhere are three different achievements.

Section: 1.3.6 · EXPLICIT REPRESENTATION
Source mapping: original slide(s) 15.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
Take the unsigned value 0x01020304 and assume an environment with eight-bit bytes and a 32-bit unsigned value representation for this example. Its four byte values can be ordered most-significant first or least-significant first. The table defines both sequences explicitly. A protocol that chooses most-significant byte first specifies the bytes independently of the sender's internal order.

This is an illustrative serialization design, not a universal rule that every protocol uses one byte order. A complete format also defines field widths, versioning where needed, and the meaning of the values. Copying an entire in-memory structure can accidentally export padding, alignment-dependent layout, or process-local addresses. The original chapter's instruction to serialize explicitly means that the external representation deserves its own contract. The receiver should not have to share an undocumented compiler or platform choice to interpret the data.

Sixth-grade explanation
When two computers share a number, they need the same packing rules. Agree on the order of the bytes instead of guessing from memory.

Section: WORKED EXAMPLE · CORRECTNESS VS. PERFORMANCE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 19.

Graduate lecture narration
The original deck compares two checksum versions using twelve and eight milliseconds. Those numbers are an illustrative comparison in the supplied teaching material, not benchmark measurements collected for this revision. Version A produces the expected checksum and has no known contract violation under the stated test. Version B appears to produce the checksum but reads beyond its buffer.

The smaller timing does not repair Version B's invalid access. We should also avoid overstating the evidence for Version A: passing the stated check does not by itself prove correctness for every input. The appropriate conclusion is narrower. Version A has passed the specified observation, while Version B has an identified rule violation and cannot be accepted as a valid optimization of the same contract. Repair the semantic issue first, then rerun correctness checks and compare performance under a controlled method.

Sixth-grade explanation
Finishing a race faster does not count if you cut across a forbidden area. A program must obey its rules before speed can make it better.

Transition: Different evidence answers different questions.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: ORIGINAL REVIEW QUESTION · DEFINED BEHAVIOR
Source mapping: original slide(s) 21, 19.

Graduate lecture narration
The source deck asks whether a run that prints the right number but reads beyond an array boundary is evidence of language-level correctness. The answer is no. The observation tells us what was printed on that execution, but the invalid access contradicts the relevant language-level obligation. We cannot use the favorable output to establish that the operation was valid.

A graduate answer should also say what to do next. Identify the access, reconstruct the valid range and lifetime, and repair the path so that it satisfies the contract. Add boundary tests and suitable runtime checks where useful, while recognizing their limits. Only then should the revised implementation be compared for performance. This response does not deny the usefulness of tests; it gives them the correct scope. Observed output is evidence about an observation, not a substitute for defined behavior.

Sixth-grade explanation
Getting the right answer once does not prove the steps were allowed. Reading outside an array still breaks the program’s rules.

Discussion / pause
What did the successful-looking output actually establish?

Expected response: Only that the expected value was observed on that run; it did not make the invalid access legal.

Transition: Graduate review: a symbol can link despite incompatible types.

C11 draft reference, not the published C17 standard. Lab examples use C17 mode. https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf
[ASAN] Clang documentation, AddressSanitizer. Runtime memory-error checking and instrumentation use. https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html

Section: SYNTHESIS · API, ABI & LINKING
Source mapping: original slide(s) 6, 9, 11, 16.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
Imagine two translation units that do not share a consistent header. The caller sees convert declared with a double parameter, while the definition in the other translation unit takes an int. An ordinary symbol-oriented link may match the name without rejecting the incompatible source types. That does not make the resulting call valid. The source-level declarations disagree, and the binary argument conventions can disagree as a result.

This is an analysis scenario, not an instruction to execute an invalid program and predict its value. A strong answer identifies the missing shared interface discipline and explains why link success is insufficient evidence. The practical repair is to provide one correct shared declaration, rebuild the affected units, and verify that the implementation and callers use it. More diagnostic tooling may help, but the contract must be coherent before tools can validate the intended composition.

Sixth-grade explanation
Two pieces may use the same function name but disagree about what to pass. Matching names alone does not make the pieces fit.

Discussion / pause
Which repair addresses the cause rather than the symptom?

Expected response: Use a correct shared declaration in both translation units, rebuild affected objects, and verify the complete interface contract.

Section: TAKEAWAYS & CHAPTER 2 PREVIEW
Source mapping: original slide(s) 22.

Graduate lecture narration
Return to the original chapter's takeaways. Computer systems are layered contracts, not one undifferentiated machine. API, ABI, and ISA describe different interfaces. Source passes through preprocessing, compilation, assembly, linking, loading, and runtime execution. Systems work makes representation, ownership, failure, and platform assumptions explicit. Correctness and performance are different properties, and each requires appropriate evidence.

The graduate addition is a method for making these statements operational. State a contract, name assumptions, predict an observation, inspect the relevant artifact, and explain what the result does and does not establish. A computer works because its parts follow shared rules. Good programmers check those rules, watch the handoffs, and plan for failures.

1.transcript:
Systems Programming and Machine Organization
Chapter 1 — Understanding Computer Systems
Charles Dorner | Graduate lecture with sixth-grade explanations

This script corresponds to the 64-slide PowerPoint. The full narration is also embedded in PowerPoint speaker notes. The visible explanations are repeated here so the script can be used without Presenter View.

Source basis: the supplied 22-slide Chapter 1 deck. Graduate elaborations are identified; the lecture does not claim to cover unseen material elsewhere in the book.

Suggested delivery: approximately 90–120 minutes including demonstrations and discussion. This is a planning estimate, not a recorded duration. Slides 61–64 are appendices.

Teaching environment: hosted C17 on Linux/ELF with a GCC-compatible compiler and GNU Binutils. Examples are educational, and their stated preconditions matter. The 12 ms / 8 ms comparison and other timing-model numbers are illustrative, not measurements of the included program.

Slide-by-slide lecture

01. Understanding Computer Systems
Section: CHAPTER 1 · GRADUATE LECTURE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 1.

Graduate lecture narration
A useful systems explanation is more precise than saying that the computer runs the code. We want to identify which component translates a representation, which component owns a resource, and which interface guarantees a particular result. Chapter 1 gives us the mental model for doing that. We will follow a small C program from source files to observable output, then ask what build success, a successful launch, and a successful test actually establish. These are different claims.

The supplied 22-slide chapter is our coverage baseline. This expanded lecture retains its organization and examples. Graduate elaborations add explicit assumptions, counterexamples, artifact inspection, and short derivations. The simplified explanation at the bottom of every slide restates the same idea without replacing the technical account. Our recurring question is: what is promised at this boundary, and what evidence would show that the promise was kept?

Sixth-grade explanation
A program is not just a list of commands. Many parts work together, and each part has rules the others must follow.

Transition: The complete Chapter 1 route.

---

02. The complete Chapter 1 route
Section: SCOPE & LEARNING OUTCOMES
Source mapping: original slide(s) 2, 7, 13, 20, 21, 22.

Graduate lecture narration
The first section distinguishes hardware, systems software, and application software, then separates API, ABI, and ISA contracts. The second section follows every stage named in the original chapter: source, preprocessing, compilation, assembly, linking, loading, and runtime execution. The third section develops the six concerns that make systems programming distinctive: representation, performance, resources, correctness, robustness, and portability.

We will retain the two-file addition program, the build-stage experiment, the expression trace, the correctness-versus-performance comparison, the guided lab, and both original review questions. The standard for graduate work is explanation with evidence. You should be able to predict which artifact contains a missing symbol, distinguish a mapping from physical residency, and state an invariant that survives an error path. The lab platform is a hosted C17 program on Linux with a GCC-compatible compiler and GNU binary tools. Other environments require corresponding tools and conventions.

Sixth-grade explanation
We will learn what the computer contains, how code becomes a running program, and how to check that the program behaves safely.

Transition: Turn a claim into a testable argument.

---

03. Turn a claim into a testable argument
Section: GRADUATE METHOD
Source mapping: original slide(s) 2, 5, 19.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
Consider the statement that our program printed 42. It reports an observation, but it does not specify the input domain, the compiler assumptions, or whether an invalid memory access occurred on the way to that output. A stronger argument separates a contract, assumptions, and evidence. The contract says what counts as correct. Assumptions identify the conditions under which the reasoning applies. Evidence is what we inspected or measured.

These categories prevent two common mistakes. First, a useful test result is not a universal proof. Second, a documented guarantee is not a measured performance result. During the lecture, attach each conclusion to its boundary: language, binary interface, operating system, or hardware. If the observation conflicts with the prediction, revise the model or inspect a lower-level artifact rather than inventing a promise that the interface never made. This framework is an instructional elaboration of the original chapter's contract model.

Sixth-grade explanation
Do not stop at “it worked.” Say what you expected, what had to be true, and what you checked.

Discussion / pause
What is missing from the claim “the executable ran successfully”?

Expected response: The success criterion, input domain, environmental assumptions, and evidence beyond that one run.

Transition: Hardware: compute, state, and movement.

---

04. Hardware: compute, state, and movement
Section: 1.1.1 · HARDWARE & SOFTWARE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 3.

Graduate lecture narration
The original chapter begins with a deliberately simplified CPU-memory-I/O model. CPU cores execute instructions, registers hold working state, memory holds addressable instructions and data, and controllers connect devices to the rest of the machine. Storage and peripherals have different purposes and access mechanisms from registers. Buses and interconnects carry requests and data among these components.

Use this picture to ask three questions: where does a value currently exist, which component initiates its movement, and what event tells another component that progress occurred? The picture is not a claim that contemporary processors execute one instruction at a time or that all transfers pass through one physical wire. It is a model of responsibilities. The software side supplies instructions and data, while the language, executable format, operating system, and device interface assign meaning to particular encodings. A sequence of bits does not identify its own type or purpose.

Sixth-grade explanation
The processor does the work. Registers and memory hold information. Controllers help the computer talk to storage and other devices.

Discussion / pause
Does a byte sequence tell you whether it is an instruction, an integer, or text?

Expected response: No. Its interpretation depends on the surrounding interface, representation, and execution context.

Transition: Follow the value—not just the statement.

---

05. Follow the value—not just the statement
Section: 1.1.1 · CPU, REGISTERS & MEMORY
Source mapping: original slide(s) 3, 18.

Graduate lecture narration
Suppose a source expression adds three to a value. Before discussing the addition, ask how the value became available to the executing instruction. It might arrive in an argument register, come from a prior calculation, or require a load. The result might remain in a register, be used immediately, or be stored. This is why a source variable should not automatically be imagined as a permanently assigned RAM slot.

The instruction stream also has to be fetched. Therefore, saying that an addition needs no data-memory access is not the same as saying that the processor uses no memory-related machinery. The original chapter makes this distinction in its expression example. Our register-workbench analogy explains placement, not exact timing or physical implementation. At this stage, track architectural inputs and outputs and leave detailed cache behavior and processor scheduling to later chapters.

Sixth-grade explanation
Think of registers as a tiny workbench and memory as a larger set of shelves. A value may already be on the workbench when it is needed.

Discussion / pause
Can the addition itself avoid a data-memory load?

Expected response: Yes, when the needed operand is already in a register or the compiler can otherwise supply it without a load.

Transition: Controllers and interrupts coordinate I/O.

---

06. Controllers and interrupts coordinate I/O
Section: 1.1.1 · STORAGE & PERIPHERALS
Source mapping: original slide(s) 3, 12.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
I/O introduces a boundary between requesting work and completing work. A controller supplies a device-facing interface. Systems software translates a higher-level request into actions the device supports. An interrupt is one mechanism by which the system can learn that an event needs attention; it should not be mistaken for the application itself performing the hardware operation.

A useful explanation identifies the requester, the component doing the transfer, and the component reporting completion. Do not silently assume that a library call corresponds to one device command or that returning from a high-level call means durable storage has been achieved. Those are separate contracts. The source deck names controllers and interrupts; this slide makes the request/completion distinction explicit without prescribing one device protocol. We will revisit the same distinction when we discuss buffered output and partial failures.

Sixth-grade explanation
A device does not always finish right away. The program asks for work, the device does it, and the system reports what happened.

Transition: Software role is not execution privilege.

---

07. Software role is not execution privilege
Section: 1.1.2–1.1.3 · SOFTWARE CATEGORIES
Source mapping: original slide(s) 4.

Graduate lecture narration
The chapter classifies systems software by role: kernels control resources, compilers translate, linkers connect compiled units, runtime libraries supply startup and shared operations, and drivers handle device-specific interactions. Application software performs tasks for users or services. The distinction is useful, but not absolute. A database application may contain its own allocator, scheduler, or storage engine.

Execution privilege is a different axis. A compiler is systems software that normally executes as an ordinary user process. A server may manage important information without becoming kernel code. Conversely, a particular driver architecture can place components on either side of a privilege boundary. Avoid using the labels low-level, systems, and privileged as synonyms. For diagnosis, ask what a component is responsible for and what operations it is authorized to perform. These questions may have different answers.

Sixth-grade explanation
Some programs help the computer run other programs. That does not mean they all get special permission to control the machine.

Discussion / pause
Why does a compiler not need kernel privilege just because it is systems software?

Expected response: Translation is its role; the OS can provide ordinary process permissions sufficient to read inputs and write outputs.

Transition: An abstraction is a smaller contract.

---

08. An abstraction is a smaller contract
Section: 1.1.4 · ABSTRACTION LAYERS
Source mapping: original slide(s) 5.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The original slide describes an abstraction as hiding detail while preserving a contract. For example, a file descriptor lets a caller request byte-oriented I/O without manipulating a storage controller. A vector presents a sequence while hiding many allocation decisions. Hidden details continue to exist; they are simply not all part of the caller's interface.

At graduate level, describe a contract using preconditions, permitted effects, postconditions, and failure behavior. Preconditions tell the caller what must already hold. Postconditions constrain the result when the operation succeeds. Failure behavior says what may have changed and what remains valid. This is a reasoning framework, not a claim that every real interface documents all of these perfectly. A missing or ambiguous guarantee is something to investigate, not permission to assume convenient behavior. Abstraction succeeds when the smaller contract is sufficient for the caller's reasoning.

Sixth-grade explanation
A button can be easy to use even when the machine behind it is complicated. You still need to know what pressing the button promises.

Transition: Guaranteed, customary, or measured?.

---

09. Guaranteed, customary, or measured?
Section: 1.1.4 · DO NOT INVENT GUARANTEES
Source mapping: original slide(s) 5, 15, 19.

Graduate lecture narration
Separate what an interface promises from what an implementation commonly does and from what you observed on a particular run. This distinction appears explicitly in the source chapter. Suppose an output operation reports that it accepted some number of bytes. The count is part of that operation's result. Whether all bytes were accepted at once, when physical storage was updated, and how long the operation took are different questions.

The vector example has the same structure: a sequence interface need not expose every allocation decision. A caller who relies on an undocumented growth choice turns an implementation detail into a hidden dependency. When presenting evidence, use precise wording. Say that a run took a measured amount of time under a stated setup, not that the API promises that latency. Say that a platform documents a behavior when it actually does. The method is to classify a claim before relying on it.

Sixth-grade explanation
A rule, a habit, and something you saw once are different. A program should not treat them as the same thing.

Transition: API, ABI, and ISA answer different questions.

Supporting primary sources
[W] Linux man-pages, write(2). Byte-output results, partial writes, and limitations of a successful return. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/write.2.html

---

10. API, ABI, and ISA answer different questions
Section: 1.1.5 · HARDWARE / SOFTWARE INTERFACES
Source mapping: original slide(s) 6.

Graduate lecture narration
An API is a source-facing interface: names, operations, argument meanings, and behavioral contracts. An ABI governs compiled interoperability: calling conventions, register use, data layout, and other binary rules. An ISA describes machine operations and software-visible architectural state. These boundaries answer different questions even when one program crosses all three in a few instructions.

Use a function call as the running example. Its source declaration tells the compiler how the call is written and typed. Binary conventions tell caller and callee where to put arguments and results. The selected machine instructions must then be valid for the target architecture. Matching at one boundary does not imply matching at the others. The original chapter's three warnings remain important: identical APIs do not imply binary compatibility; a shared ISA does not imply a shared ABI; and a shared ISA does not imply identical microarchitecture or speed.

Sixth-grade explanation
The API says what you can ask for. The ABI says how compiled parts pass things. The ISA says which machine commands the processor understands.

Transition: One ISA can support different calling conventions.

---

11. One ISA can support different calling conventions
Section: 1.1.5 · ABI CASE STUDY
Source mapping: original slide(s) 6.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
Here is a concrete graduate extension of the chapter's ABI distinction. For an ordinary function taking two int parameters, a System V AMD64 caller uses the integer argument-register convention associated with RDI and RSI, with the int values in their 32-bit portions. The usual Microsoft x64 convention uses RCX and RDX for those positions instead. For the int return in this example, EAX is used in both conventions.

This is a deliberately narrow example. Real ABIs also define stack rules, preserved registers, alignment, aggregate classification, and other details. Do not extend this two-int table to every type or every function. It is enough to demonstrate the logical point: a machine can implement the x86-64 ISA while binary components disagree about how a function is called. Source-level similarity is not evidence that independently built objects can be combined safely.

Sixth-grade explanation
Two people can speak the same language but use different handoff rules. Compiled functions also need to agree on where each value goes.

Discussion / pause
Would matching instruction sets make these two calling conventions interchangeable?

Expected response: No. Caller and callee must also agree on argument locations and the rest of the binary contract.

Transition: Architecture is a promise; implementation is a choice.

Supporting primary sources
[ABI] System V AMD64 ABI, draft 0.99.6, §3.2 (2012). Ordinary integer calling conventions, register usage, and processor-specific ABI context. https://refspecs.linuxfoundation.org/elf/x86_64-abi-0.99.pdf
[MS] Microsoft Learn, x64 calling convention. Ordinary Microsoft x64 integer argument and return conventions. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/build/x64-calling-convention?view=msvc-170

---

12. Architecture is a promise; implementation is a choice
Section: 1.1.5 · ISA VS. MICROARCHITECTURE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 3, 6, 18, 19.

Graduate lecture narration
The chapter warns that an ISA and a microarchitecture are not the same thing. The ISA defines the software-visible operations and state that an implementation must honor. Microarchitecture concerns how a particular implementation realizes that behavior. The existence of the same instruction in two systems does not establish the same latency, throughput, cache behavior, or resource contention.

Keep two explanations separate. A functional explanation asks which architectural result an instruction produces under its specified conditions. A performance explanation asks how long a workload takes on a particular implementation and why. A correct functional trace does not provide enough information to derive whole-program timing. Conversely, a favorable benchmark cannot excuse an invalid instruction assumption or a violated language rule. This distinction prepares the performance discussion without turning Chapter 1 into a processor-design course.

Sixth-grade explanation
Two cars can follow the same road rules but have different engines. Two processors can run the same commands at different speeds.

Transition: Locate the boundary before proposing a fix.

---

13. Locate the boundary before proposing a fix
Section: 1.1 · INTERFACE REASONING CHECK
Source mapping: original slide(s) 6, 11, 12, 21.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
A systems failure is easier to investigate when the symptom is attached to a boundary. A missing source declaration is not the same problem as a missing compiled definition. A binary that requires a different instruction set has a different issue from a program that lacks access to a file. The table gives initial hypotheses, not a complete diagnostic decision tree.

The graduate task is to state the evidence that would discriminate among plausible explanations. For a binary-interface concern, examine build settings and the ABI of both components. For a runtime file error, inspect the operation's returned status and the relevant environment. For a performance discrepancy, record the workload and implementation. Avoid responding to every symptom by recompiling everything or increasing privileges. Those actions may hide the mismatch instead of explaining it. Later slides make the build-stage examples concrete.

Sixth-grade explanation
When something breaks, first find which handoff went wrong. Fixing the wrong part wastes time.

Transition: Seven stages, seven different questions.

---

14. Seven stages, seven different questions
Section: 1.2 · FROM SOURCE TO EXECUTION
Source mapping: original slide(s) 7.

Graduate lecture narration
The source chapter presents a seven-stage model: source, preprocessing, compilation, assembly, linking, loading, and execution. The model separates responsibilities; it does not require every implementation to launch a separate operating-system process for every stage. Compiler drivers often orchestrate several stages in a single command.

Each stage changes what kind of evidence is available. Source text exposes the programmer's operations and obligations. Preprocessed text exposes the translation unit after directives and macros. Assembly exposes symbolic target operations. An object file exposes encoded data, symbols, and relocation requirements. A linked executable describes a loadable program, while loading and runtime establish and exercise the process environment. Notice that passing an earlier stage does not guarantee passing later stages. Successful compilation does not supply an omitted definition, and successful loading does not guarantee that a runtime resource will be available.

Sixth-grade explanation
The program goes through several stations before and while it runs. Each station has a different job and can find a different kind of problem.

Transition: Source code describes an abstract computation.

Supporting primary sources
[GCC] GCC manual, Overall Options. Compilation stages and the -E, -S, -c, and -o compiler-driver options. https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Overall-Options.html

---

15. Source code describes an abstract computation
Section: 1.2.1 · SOURCE-LEVEL CONTRACT
Source mapping: original slide(s) 8.

Graduate lecture narration
Before imagining instructions, identify the source-level semantics. The original chapter lists types, expressions, statements, lifetimes, synchronization rules, and observable behavior. These constrain the abstract computation, but source order is not a literal physical schedule. A correct implementation may transform the computation while preserving the behavior required by the language and the implementation's documented guarantees.

For a pointer access, ask whether the object exists, whether the access is in range, and whether its lifetime and synchronization obligations hold. For arithmetic, ask whether the result is representable under the relevant rules. These are not optional details to check after performance tuning. They define the domain in which the rest of the explanation is valid. The public C committee draft provides a reference for abstract-machine reasoning; the lab retains the source deck's C17 compilation mode.

Sixth-grade explanation
Code has rules about what values mean and when they may be used. The computer may organize the work differently while keeping the promised result.

Transition: Not all language uncertainty is undefined behavior.

Supporting primary sources
[LANG] WG14 N1570, Programming languages — C, committee draft (2011). §3.4 behavior categories; §5.1 abstract machine and execution; §6.5 expressions; declarations and external definitions. C11 draft reference, not the published C17 standard. Lab examples use C17 mode. https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf

---

16. Not all language uncertainty is undefined behavior
Section: 1.2.1 · CLASSIFY THE RULE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 8, 19, 21.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
This classification extends the original instruction to check defined behavior first. Some behavior is directly constrained by the language rules. Other matters permit an implementation-defined choice that the implementation documents, or an unspecified choice among permitted alternatives. Undefined behavior is different: it does not provide an ordinary language-level guarantee for the erroneous execution.

For the chapter's systems model, the practical point is not memorizing labels. It is choosing the right evidence. Documentation is relevant to an implementation-defined property. A program should not depend on a particular unspecified choice unless its specification tolerates all allowed choices. An out-of-bounds access cannot be justified by reporting that a test happened to print the expected number. Be careful with scope: the labels attach to specific rules and operations, not to the vague claim that an entire compiler is unpredictable.

Sixth-grade explanation
Sometimes a rule allows a choice. Sometimes the maker must explain the choice. Breaking a rule is different from either kind of choice.

Transition: Preprocessing works on directives and tokens.

Supporting primary sources
[LANG] WG14 N1570, Programming languages — C, committee draft (2011). §3.4 behavior categories; §5.1 abstract machine and execution; §6.5 expressions; declarations and external definitions. C11 draft reference, not the published C17 standard. Lab examples use C17 mode. https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf

---

17. Preprocessing works on directives and tokens
Section: 1.2.2 · HEADERS, MACROS & CONDITIONALS
Source mapping: original slide(s) 9.

Graduate lecture narration
The original preprocessing example contains a standard header, a macro constant, and a platform conditional. Include processing makes header content available to the translation unit; it does not automatically cause an external function implementation to be linked into the final program. Conditional inclusion is a translation-time decision. It is not a runtime test executed each time the program runs.

Macros operate on preprocessing tokens. They are not typed runtime variables or ordinary function calls. That distinction matters when an argument contains an operation with a side effect, as the next slide demonstrates. Use the preprocessed file as evidence when a macro or a conditional produces surprising source code. This is a more direct method than guessing at what the compiler saw. The platform symbol in this example is explicitly environment-specific, which also connects preprocessing to portability assumptions.

Sixth-grade explanation
Before normal compilation, the preprocessor follows special instructions, brings in header text, and replaces chosen words or symbols.

Transition: A macro can duplicate an operation.

Supporting primary sources
[GCC] GCC manual, Overall Options. Compilation stages and the -E, -S, -c, and -o compiler-driver options. https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Overall-Options.html
[CPP] GNU C Preprocessor, Duplication of Side Effects. Token substitution and unsafe repeated evaluation in macros. https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/cpp/Duplication-of-Side-Effects.html

---

18. A macro can duplicate an operation
Section: 1.2.2 · PREPROCESSOR COUNTEREXAMPLE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 9.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
This is a deliberately invalid example for analysis, not a program to use as a numerical experiment. The SQUARE macro replaces its parameter in two positions. Giving it i++ expands the increment expression twice. In C, the two modifications shown in the multiplication expression are unsequenced relative to one another, so the example has undefined behavior. There is no correct portable numeric answer to predict.

Parentheses are still useful in macros because they prevent some precedence surprises, but they do not make repeated evaluation safe. A function that receives an already computed value separates the caller's side effect from the body calculation. Even then, arithmetic range requirements remain: replacing the macro with a function does not make arbitrary signed multiplication overflow valid. This extension turns the source deck's warning about duplicated side effects into a concrete contract failure.

Sixth-grade explanation
A macro can copy your instruction more than once. Asking it to “use the number and then increase it” can accidentally copy the increase too.

Discussion / pause
What portable value should we predict for y?

Expected response: None. The shown expanded expression violates C sequencing rules.

Transition: Declarations enable checking; definitions supply entities.

Supporting primary sources
[CPP] GNU C Preprocessor, Duplication of Side Effects. Token substitution and unsafe repeated evaluation in macros. https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/cpp/Duplication-of-Side-Effects.html
[LANG] WG14 N1570, Programming languages — C, committee draft (2011). §3.4 behavior categories; §5.1 abstract machine and execution; §6.5 expressions; declarations and external definitions. C11 draft reference, not the published C17 standard. Lab examples use C17 mode. https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf

---

19. Declarations enable checking; definitions supply entities
Section: 1.2.2 · TRANSLATION UNITS
Source mapping: original slide(s) 9, 16.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
In the chapter's two-file program, sum.h declares add, sum.c defines it, and main.c calls it. The declaration lets each translation unit check source-level uses. The compiled caller can still depend on a definition that will be supplied later. That is the central reason a program may compile and then fail at the link stage.

The graduate nuance is that a header is not intrinsically declaration-only. Headers can also contain definitions, subject to language and linkage rules. Our teaching layout places this externally linked function's declaration in the header and its definition in one source file. The include guard in the companion lab is an added organizational aid. Distinguish a file's conventional role from a language restriction. Also remember that consistent declarations across translation units are a programmer and build-system responsibility; a conventional linker is not a complete source-level type checker.

Sixth-grade explanation
A declaration says that a function exists and how to call it. A definition contains the actual function body.

Transition: The compiler transforms meaning into a target program.

42. Ownership turns resources into explicit obligations

The chapter says every acquisition needs an owner, a validity interval, and a release rule. 48. Portability has at least three separate targets
Section: 1.3.6 · PORTABILITY
Source mapping: original slide(s) 15.

Graduate lecture narration
The original chapter explicitly distinguishes source portability, binary compatibility, and performance portability. Source portability concerns whether the program can be translated appropriately for another supported environment. Binary compatibility concerns whether compiled components can interoperate or execute under the expected machine and runtime conventions. Performance portability concerns whether the implementation still meets the relevant performance goals across platforms.

These are related but independent claims. A portable source program may need rebuilding. A binary can require a particular ABI or shared library. A program that executes correctly may have different bottlenecks on a second implementation. Make each platform assumption visible and testable: representation, interfaces, resource limits, compiler options, and runtime dependencies. Do not call a design portable without specifying the supported environments and the level of portability being claimed.

Sixth-grade explanation
Code that can be rebuilt elsewhere, a file that runs elsewhere, and a program that stays fast elsewhere are three different achievements.
